summary: For ages 5–6 (Year 1 / Kindergarten), learners compare two written numerals from 1 to 10 and decide which is greater or less, using the words 'greater than / less than' and later the symbols >, <, =. The central idea is that a numeral stands for an amount: comparison must be grounded in quantity or number-line position, not in how the symbol looks on the page. The number line acts as the arbiter (further right = greater), and >, < are introduced as a sign that opens toward the larger number — introduced only after the quantity meaning is secure, and never reduced to a meaning-free 'hungry alligator' trick. Equality (=) is kept as a genuine third outcome.
misconceptions: Comparing the numerals as marks (which looks bigger / is written larger) rather than by value.
Using <, > by mnemonic with no meaning → placing the symbol backwards.
Assuming a later-learned or longer-to-say numeral is automatically bigger; confusing 'greater' with physical size.
Forgetting '=' is a possible result (assuming one number must be bigger).

activities.title: Anchor the numeral to its amount, then compare on a number line
steps: Take two numeral cards, for example 4 and 7, and place each on a number line marked 1–10.
Beside each numeral build or reveal its quantity — a little tower of cubes, counters, or a filled ten-frame — so the amount behind the symbol is visible.
Say which is further along the line when you count, and therefore which is greater and which is less.
State the comparison out loud in BOTH directions: '7 is greater than 4 AND 4 is less than 7.'
Repeat with pairs that include an equal pair (for example 5 and 5) so you meet all three outcomes.
activities.insight: A written numeral names an amount; you compare the amounts, and the number line settles it because the numeral further right is greater. Equality is a possible result, so comparison has three outcomes (>, <, =).

activities.title: Place the >, < or = sign: > and < open toward the larger amount, = shows the amounts are the same
steps: Keep the two numerals (with their towers/quantities visible) on the number line.
Choose and place the correct sign between them: >, <, or =.
Check the sign by its open end — the wide, open end should face the larger numeral/tower; the point faces the smaller.
Read the finished statement aloud exactly as written, for example '4 < 7' as 'four is less than seven'.
If what you read aloud does not match which number is actually bigger, flip the sign and read it again.
Try equal pairs so you also place the = sign.
activities.insight: The comparison sign is not a picture to memorise: when the amounts differ, the open end of > or < always faces the larger amount — the numeral further along the number line — and when they are the same, = is used. Reading the completed statement aloud is how you check it is correct.

activities.title: Compare and order from the numerals alone
steps: Given single-digit numeral pairs with no objects present — for example 4 __ 7, 9 __ 6, 3 __ 8 — decide for each which is greater or less and place the correct sign.
Read each completed comparison aloud ('four is less than seven', 'nine is greater than six', 'three is less than eight').
Answer 'which of 5 and 2 is smaller?' working directly from the numerals.
Put a short set of single-digit numerals in order from least to greatest.
Say how you know, using number-line position ('8 is further along when you count than 3').
activities.insight: Once the numeral-to-amount link is secure you can compare and order written numerals directly, without first building sets, and justify it by where each sits on the number line.

activities.title: Talk it through: who has more, and how do you know?
steps: Given two numerals or two small collections, say which represents more and explain your reasoning.
Use the words 'greater than', 'less than', and 'equal to' in your explanation.
Respond to follow-up questions such as 'which is further along when you count?' and 'could they ever be the same?'
activities.insight: Putting the comparison into words, including the possibility of equality, strengthens the link between the spoken comparison language and the written symbols.

checkQuestion: Look at these pairs of written numbers. For each pair, put the right sign between them — greater than or less than — and read it aloud to me: 4 __ 7, then 9 __ 6, then 3 __ 8. Then tell me which of 5 and 2 is smaller. (Watch whether they work from the numerals alone, orient the sign correctly, and handle 'smaller'.)
checkAnswer: 4 < 7, 9 > 6, 3 < 8, read correctly ('4 is less than 7' etc.); and identifies 2 as smaller than 5 — working directly from the numerals.
